claim: When placed on a spatial thermal gradient, well-fed but not food-deprived C. elegans navigates toward temperatures at which they were cultivated (Tc) for 3–4 hr prior to the behavioral assay.
source: When placed on a spatial thermal gradient, well-fed but not food-deprived C. elegans navigates toward temperatures at which they were cultivated (Tc) for 3–4 hr prior to the behavioral assay (Figure 1A; Hedgecock and Russell, 1975).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hedgecock and Russell, 1975, and reference to Figure 1A which shows the schematic of the behavior.

claim: Thermosensation is mediated primarily by the AFD sensory neurons and their major postsynaptic partners, the AIY interneurons in the head of C. elegans.
source: Thermosensation is mediated primarily by the AFD sensory neurons, and their major postsynaptic partners, the AIY interneurons in the head of C. elegans (Mori and Ohshima, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mori and Ohshima, 1995.

claim: Additional sensory neurons including the AWC olfactory neurons exhibit temperature responses but play relatively minor roles in regulating thermotaxis behaviors under standard assay conditions.
source: Additional sensory neurons including the AWC olfactory neurons also exhibit temperature responses but play relatively minor roles in regulating thermotaxis behaviors under standard assay conditions (Biron et al., 2008; Ikeda et al., 2020; Kuhara et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Biron et al., 2008; Ikeda et al., 2020; Kuhara et al., 2008.

claim: Temperature responses in AFD appear to be indifferent to feeding state.
source: Temperature responses in AFD appear to be indifferent to feeding state (Biron et al., 2006; Ramot et al., 2008a; Tsukada et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Biron et al., 2006; Ramot et al., 2008a; Tsukada et al., 2016.

claim: The INS-1 insulin-like peptide gene was suggested to antagonize the DAF-2 insulin receptor and the DAF-16/FOXO transcription factor to disrupt thermotaxis behavior upon food deprivation.
source: The INS-1 insulin-like peptide (ILP) gene was suggested to antagonize the DAF-2 insulin receptor and the DAF-16/FOXO transcription factor to disrupt thermotaxis behavior upon food deprivation, such that starved ins-1 mutants continue to perform thermotaxis (Kodama et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kodama et al., 2006.

claim: Feeding state alters C. elegans thermotaxis behavior by engaging a modulatory circuit whose activity gates the output of the core thermotaxis network.
source: Here we show that feeding state alters C. elegans thermotaxis behavior by engaging a modulatory circuit whose activity gates the output of the core thermotaxis network.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Feeding state does not alter the activity of the core thermotaxis circuit comprised of AFD thermosensory and AIY interneurons.
source: Feeding state does not alter the activity of the core thermotaxis circuit comprised of AFD thermosensory and AIY interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 1E-G.

claim: Prolonged food deprivation potentiates temperature responses in the AWC sensory neurons.
source: Instead, prolonged food deprivation potentiates temperature responses in the AWC sensory neurons, which inhibit the postsynaptic AIA interneurons to override and disrupt AFD-driven thermotaxis behavior.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2C.

claim: AWC sensory neurons inhibit the postsynaptic AIA interneurons to override and disrupt AFD-driven thermotaxis behavior upon starvation.
source: Instead, prolonged food deprivation potentiates temperature responses in the AWC sensory neurons, which inhibit the postsynaptic AIA interneurons to override and disrupt AFD-driven thermotaxis behavior.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by behavioral and imaging data in Figures 2-3.

claim: Acute inhibition of AWC restores negative thermotaxis in starved animals.
source: Acute inhibition and activation of AWC and AIA, respectively, restores negative thermotaxis in starved animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by optogenetic and chemogenetic manipulation data in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Acute activation of AIA restores negative thermotaxis in starved animals.
source: Acute inhibition and activation of AWC and AIA, respectively, restores negative thermotaxis in starved animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by optogenetic activation data in Figure 3H.

claim: State-dependent modulation of AWC-AIA temperature responses requires INS-1 insulin-like peptide signaling from the gut.
source: We find that state-dependent modulation of AWC-AIA temperature responses requires INS-1 insulin-like peptide signaling from the gut and DAF-16/FOXO function in AWC.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by cell-specific knockout and imaging data in Figure 4.

claim: State-dependent modulation of AWC-AIA temperature responses requires DAF-16/FOXO function in AWC.
source: We find that state-dependent modulation of AWC-AIA temperature responses requires INS-1 insulin-like peptide signaling from the gut and DAF-16/FOXO function in AWC.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by auxin-induced degradation data in Figure 4E.

claim: Well-fed young adult hermaphrodites grown at 15°C and placed at 20°C on a long thermal gradient moved robustly down the gradient toward cooler temperatures.
source: Well-fed young adult hermaphrodites grown at 15°C, and placed at 20°C at the center of a shallow linear thermal gradient (long thermal gradient; see Materials and methods), moved robustly down the gradient toward cooler temperatures (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Animals grown at 25°C and placed at 20°C on a long thermal gradient moved toward warmer temperatures.
source: Conversely, animals grown at 25°C and placed at 20°C on this gradient moved toward warmer temperatures (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Food deprivation for 3 hr disrupted both negative and positive thermotaxis navigation behaviors.
source: Food deprivation for 3 hr disrupted both navigation behaviors (Figure 1B; Chi et al., 2007; Ramot et al., 2008b).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 1B and citations to Chi et al., 2007; Ramot et al., 2008b.

claim: Food-deprived animals grown at 15°C exhibited more sharp turns and reversals than their fed counterparts.
source: In particular, examination of individual animal trajectories showed that food-deprived animals grown at 15°C exhibited more sharp turns and reversals than their fed counterparts, resulting in prolonged residence at the starting temperature.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of behavioral trajectories shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Starvation-dependent modulation of navigation behaviors was observed only on thermal gradients.
source: Starvation-dependent modulation of navigation behaviors was observed only on thermal gradients; fed and starved animals exhibited similar velocities and dispersed throughout an isothermal plate held at 20°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data on isothermal plates shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Fed and starved animals exhibited similar velocities on isothermal plates held at 20°C.
source: Starvation-dependent modulation of navigation behaviors was observed only on thermal gradients; fed and starved animals exhibited similar velocities and dispersed throughout an isothermal plate held at 20°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: On spatial thermal gradients, negative thermotaxis is mediated primarily via klinokinesis.
source: On spatial thermal gradients, negative thermotaxis is mediated primarily via klinokinesis (Clark et al., 2007; Luo et al., 2014a; Ryu and Samuel, 2002; Zariwala et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clark et al., 2007; Luo et al., 2014a; Ryu and Samuel, 2002; Zariwala et al., 2003.

claim: In klinokinesis, worms moving toward cooler temperatures suppress reorientations (turns) and consequently extend the duration of forward movement (runs).
source: In this behavioral strategy, worms moving toward cooler temperatures suppress reorientations (turns) and consequently, extend the duration of forward movement (runs).
evidence: This describes the klinokinesis behavioral strategy, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: When moving toward the non-preferred warmer temperatures, worms increase turn frequency and decrease run duration.
source: Conversely, when moving toward the non-preferred warmer temperatures, worms increase turn frequency and decrease run duration.
evidence: This describes the klinokinesis behavioral strategy, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Following a turn, worms preferentially bias the direction of a new run toward cooler temperatures.
source: In parallel, following a turn, worms preferentially bias the direction of a new run toward cooler temperatures (Luo et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2014a.

claim: Well-fed animals exhibited robust negative thermotaxis bias on short thermal gradients.
source: While well-fed animals exhibited robust negative thermotaxis bias under these conditions, animals starved for >2 hr were essentially athermotactic, indicating that these animals were unable to modulate turning frequency as a function of experienced temperature changes (Figure 1C; Chi et al., 2007; Hedgecock and Russell, 1975; Kodama et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by thermotaxis bias data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Animals starved for >2 hr were essentially athermotactic.
source: While well-fed animals exhibited robust negative thermotaxis bias under these conditions, animals starved for >2 hr were essentially athermotactic, indicating that these animals were unable to modulate turning frequency as a function of experienced temperature changes (Figure 1C; Chi et al., 2007; Hedgecock and Russell, 1975; Kodama et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by thermotaxis bias data shown in Figure 1C and citations to Chi et al., 2007; Hedgecock and Russell, 1975; Kodama et al., 2006.

claim: Starved animals failed to orient run direction toward cooler temperatures following a turn, and instead oriented their runs near-randomly on the gradient.
source: We established that starved animals also failed to orient run direction toward cooler temperatures following a turn, and instead oriented their runs near-randomly on the gradient (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by orientation analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Average velocities of fed and starved animals were indistinguishable on short thermal gradients.
source: Average velocities of fed and starved animals were indistinguishable on these gradients (average velocity: fed – 117 μm/s, starved for 3 hr – 106 μm/s; n = 10 animals each).
evidence: The claim is supported by velocity measurements reported in the text.

claim: Prolonged starvation abolishes both klinokinesis and biased run direction to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
source: Together, these observations indicate that prolonged starvation abolishes both klinokinesis and biased run direction to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data showing loss of both turning modulation and directional bias.

claim: Refeeding starved animals for an hour was sufficient to restore robust negative thermotaxis bias.
source: Refeeding starved animals for an hour was sufficient to restore robust negative thermotaxis bias (Figure 1C; Chi et al., 2007; Mohri et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by refeeding data shown in Figure 1C and citations to Chi et al., 2007; Mohri et al., 2005.

claim: Prolonged starvation does not irreversibly alter the function of the thermotaxis circuit.
source: Refeeding starved animals for an hour was sufficient to restore robust negative thermotaxis bias (Figure 1C; Chi et al., 2007; Mohri et al., 2005), indicating that prolonged starvation does not irreversibly alter the function of the underlying circuit.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the refeeding experiment showing reversibility of the starvation effect.

claim: The presence of bacteria on the lids of agar plates did not override the effect of starvation on negative thermotaxis.
source: However, the presence of bacteria on the lids of agar plates did not override the effect of starvation on negative thermotaxis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Feeding animals either live or antibiotic-killed bacteria was sufficient to mimic the well-fed condition for negative thermotaxis.
source: Moreover, feeding animals either live or antibiotic-killed bacteria was sufficient to mimic the well-fed condition for negative thermotaxis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Prolonged starvation alters internal state to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
source: We infer that prolonged starvation alters internal state to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experiments showing that bacterial odors alone are insufficient and that feeding (live or dead bacteria) is necessary.

claim: AFD responds to temperature changes above a Tc-determined threshold referred to as T*AFD.
source: AFD responds to temperature changes above a Tc-determined threshold referred to as T*AFD (Clark et al., 2006; Kimura et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clark et al., 2006; Kimura et al., 2004.

claim: Temperature-driven calcium dynamics in AFD were largely indifferent to feeding state.
source: Confirming and extending previous observations using different temperature stimulus paradigms (Biron et al., 2006; Matsuyama and Mori, 2020; Ramot et al., 2008a; Tsukada et al., 2016), we found that temperature-driven calcium dynamics in AFD were largely indifferent to feeding state, although we noted a small but statistically significant decrease in T*AFD upon starvation (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1E and citations to Biron et al., 2006; Matsuyama and Mori, 2020; Ramot et al., 2008a; Tsukada et al., 2016.

claim: There was a small but statistically significant decrease in T*AFD upon starvation.
source: Confirming and extending previous observations using different temperature stimulus paradigms (Biron et al., 2006; Matsuyama and Mori, 2020; Ramot et al., 2008a; Tsukada et al., 2016), we found that temperature-driven calcium dynamics in AFD were largely indifferent to feeding state, although we noted a small but statistically significant decrease in T*AFD upon starvation (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by T*AFD measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The observed change in T*AFD is unlikely to drive starvation-induced loss of negative thermotaxis behavior.
source: Since manipulations resulting in effects of a similar magnitude on T*AFD do not disrupt negative thermotaxis (Inada et al., 2006; Takeishi et al., 2016; Wasserman et al., 2011), we infer that the observed change in T*AFD is unlikely to drive starvation-induced loss of negative thermotaxis behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previous studies showing that similar magnitude changes in T*AFD do not affect thermotaxis.

claim: Food deprivation has been suggested to alter the phase relationship between AFD and AIY temperature responses in a restricted temperature range.
source: In a recent study, food deprivation has been suggested to alter the phase relationship between AFD and AIY temperature responses in a restricted temperature range and may mediate plasticity in positive thermotaxis (Matsuyama and Mori, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Matsuyama and Mori, 2020.

claim: Stochastic calcium transients were observed in AIY neurons in response to a shallow linear temperature ramp.
source: In contrast to the robust and deterministic temperature responses observed in AFD, we observed stochastic calcium transients in AIY neurons expressing GCaMP6s in immobilized animals in response to the shallow linear temperature ramp (Figure 1F) (also see Hawk et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1F and citation to Hawk et al., 2018.

claim: No significant differences in total response duration per neuron or the average duration of individual response bouts in AIY were observed between fed and starved animals.
source: We observed no significant differences in total response duration per neuron or the average duration of individual response bouts in AIY between fed and starved animals (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of AIY calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The proportion of AIY neurons responding to the rising temperature stimulus in the temperature range of the behavioral assay (23–28°C) was similar under fed and starved conditions.
source: Moreover, the proportion of AIY neurons responding to the rising temperature stimulus in the temperature range of the behavioral assay (23–28°C) was similar under fed and starved conditions, although we noted that responses were initiated at a lower temperature in a subset of AIY neurons upon starvation (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of AIY calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Temperature responses in AIY can be driven by thermal inputs from sensory neurons other than AFD.
source: Temperature responses in AIY can be driven by thermal inputs from sensory neurons other than AFD (Biron et al., 2008; Hawk et al., 2018; Kuhara et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Biron et al., 2008; Hawk et al., 2018; Kuhara et al., 2008.

claim: The frequency of responses in AIY in the peri-Tc temperature range was similar in fed and starved animals.
source: We found that the frequency of responses in this temperature range in AIY was also similar in fed and starved animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of AIY responses near Tc shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: AFD thermosensory responses and likely AFD synaptic output as measured by responses in AIY are largely unaffected by starvation.
source: We conclude that AFD thermosensory responses, and likely AFD synaptic output as measured by responses in AIY, are largely unaffected by starvation, and that alternate pathways incorporate internal state information elsewhere in the thermotaxis circuit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AFD and AIY imaging data showing minimal changes with starvation.

claim: AWC responds robustly to food-related volatile odors.
source: AWC responds robustly to food-related volatile odors (Bargmann et al., 1993; Chalasani et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bargmann et al., 1993; Chalasani et al., 2007.

claim: AWC olfactory responses and AWC-driven behaviors are modulated by the presence or absence of bacterial food.
source: AWC olfactory responses and AWC-driven behaviors are modulated by the presence or absence of bacterial food (Chalasani et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2016; Colbert and Bargmann, 1995; Lin et al., 2010; Neal et al., 2015; Torayama et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chalasani et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2016; Colbert and Bargmann, 1995; Lin et al., 2010; Neal et al., 2015; Torayama et al., 2007.

claim: Silencing AWC during the assay alone was sufficient to restore negative thermotaxis bias in starved animals.
source: However, silencing AWC during the assay alone was sufficient to restore negative thermotaxis bias in starved animals (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by HisCl1-mediated silencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HisCl1-mediated silencing of AWC restored the ability of starved animals to bias the direction of runs following turns toward cooler temperatures.
source: Moreover, HisCl1-mediated silencing of AWC restored the ability of starved animals to bias the direction of runs following turns toward cooler temperatures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by orientation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Optogenetic silencing of AWC during the assay was sufficient to restore negative thermotaxis bias in starved animals.
source: Optogenetic silencing of AWC during the assay was again sufficient to restore negative thermotaxis bias in starved animals (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by GtACR2-mediated silencing data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Acute silencing of AWC in adult animals is sufficient to abolish starvation-dependent thermotaxis behavioral plasticity.
source: These results indicate that acute silencing of AWC in adult animals is sufficient to abolish starvation-dependent thermotaxis behavioral plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AWC silencing experiments using both HisCl1 and GtACR2.

claim: AWC activity is necessary during the execution of thermotaxis behavior to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
source: Moreover, we infer that AWC activity is necessary during the execution of thermotaxis behavior to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that silencing AWC only during the assay (not during starvation) is sufficient to restore thermotaxis.

claim: AWC neurons in fed animals exhibited relatively infrequent and stochastic calcium transients in response to a shallow rising temperature stimulus from 23–28°C.
source: AWC neurons in fed animals grown overnight at 20°C exhibited relatively infrequent and stochastic calcium transients in response to a shallow rising temperature stimulus from 23–28°C, the temperature range in which animals exhibit negative thermotaxis in our behavioral assays (see Materials and methods; Figure 2C; Biron et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C and citation to Biron et al., 2008.

claim: The total response duration per neuron as well as the average duration of individual events in AWC was significantly increased in response to a rising temperature ramp upon starvation for 3 hr.
source: However, we found that the total response duration per neuron as well as the average duration of individual events was significantly increased in response to a rising temperature ramp upon starvation for 3 hr (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging analysis shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A greater proportion of AWC neurons responded as the temperature increased in starved animals.
source: Moreover, a greater proportion of AWC neurons responded as the temperature increased in starved animals (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: AWC neuronal responses were unaltered in starved animals held at 20°C.
source: In contrast, AWC neuronal responses were unaltered in starved animals held at 20°C (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data at constant temperature shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Starvation increases responses to rising temperatures in AWC, and this increased activity is necessary to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
source: Together, these results indicate that starvation increases responses to rising temperatures in AWC, and that this increased activity is necessary to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AWC imaging and silencing experiments.

claim: Increasing AWC activity either via genetic or optogenetic means has been shown to promote reversals and turns via inhibition and activation of the postsynaptic primary layer interneurons AIY and AIA, and AIB, respectively.
source: Increasing AWC activity either via genetic or optogenetic means has previously been shown to promote reversals and turns via inhibition and activation of the postsynaptic primary layer interneurons AIY and AIA, and AIB, respectively (Figure 3A; Albrecht and Bargmann, 2011; Chalasani et al., 2007; Chalasani et al., 2010; Gordus et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; White et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Albrecht and Bargmann, 2011; Chalasani et al., 2007; Chalasani et al., 2010; Gordus et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; White et al., 1986, and reference to Figure 3A showing circuit connectivity.

claim: AIY and AIA inhibit reversals and/or turns.
source: Consequently, AIY and AIA inhibit, and AIB promotes, reversals and/or turns (Figure 3A; Chalasani et al., 2007; Gordus et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; Kocabas et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; López-Cruz et al., 2019; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Wakabayashi et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chalasani et al., 2007; Gordus et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; Kocabas et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; López-Cruz et al., 2019; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Wakabayashi et al., 2004, and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: AIB promotes reversals and/or turns.
source: Consequently, AIY and AIA inhibit, and AIB promotes, reversals and/or turns (Figure 3A; Chalasani et al., 2007; Gordus et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; Kocabas et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; López-Cruz et al., 2019; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Wakabayashi et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chalasani et al., 2007; Gordus et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; Kocabas et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; López-Cruz et al., 2019; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Wakabayashi et al., 2004, and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: AIA and AIB exhibited stochastic calcium transients in response to a shallow rising temperature stimulus in the T > Tc regime.
source: Similar to AIY, both AIA and AIB exhibited stochastic calcium transients in response to a shallow rising temperature stimulus in the T > Tc regime (Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: AIB temperature responses were similar in fed and starved animals.
source: AIB temperature responses were similar in fed and starved animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Responses to a rising temperature ramp in AIA were markedly altered upon starvation.
source: However, responses to a rising temperature ramp in AIA were markedly altered upon starvation (Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: AIA appeared to be tonically active and exhibited frequent calcium transients in fed animals subjected to either a rising temperature stimulus or a constant holding temperature of 20°C.
source: AIA appeared to be tonically active and exhibited frequent calcium transients in fed animals subjected to either a rising temperature stimulus or a constant holding temperature of 20°C (Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Upon prolonged starvation, the proportion of responding animals, the total response duration per neuron as well as the average duration of individual response bouts in AIA were significantly suppressed in response to a rising temperature ramp but not when held at 20°C.
source: However, upon prolonged starvation, the proportion of responding animals, the total response duration per neuron as well as the average duration of individual response bouts were significantly suppressed in response to a rising temperature ramp but not when held at 20°C (Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging analysis shown in Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Temperature responses in AIZ exhibited tonic stochastic activity in fed animals subjected to a rising temperature stimulus, and these responses were decreased upon starvation.
source: Under our imaging conditions, temperature responses in AIZ, like those in AIA, exhibited tonic stochastic activity in fed animals subjected to a rising temperature stimulus, and these responses were decreased upon starvation (Figure 3D–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3D–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Acute inhibition of the AIA circuit via addition of histamine to the assay plate resulted in animals exhibiting extensive reversals and turns at the starting temperature regardless of feeding state.
source: However, acute inhibition of the AIA circuit via addition of histamine to the assay plate resulted in animals exhibiting extensive reversals and turns at the starting temperature regardless of feeding state, and consequent inability of these animals to navigate the gradient (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data with HisCl1-mediated AIA inhibition shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Acute inhibition of AIZ via expression of HisCl1 and addition of histamine decreased spontaneous reversals on an isothermal plate.
source: However, although acute inhibition of AIZ via expression of HisCl1 (see Materials and methods) and addition of histamine decreased spontaneous reversals on an isothermal plate as reported previously (Gray et al., 2005; Li et al., 2014; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), AIZ inhibition had no effect on the expected thermotaxis behavior of either fed or starved animals (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by reversal frequency data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and citations to Gray et al., 2005; Li et al., 2014; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003.

claim: AIZ inhibition had no effect on the expected thermotaxis behavior of either fed or starved animals.
source: However, although acute inhibition of AIZ via expression of HisCl1 (see Materials and methods) and addition of histamine decreased spontaneous reversals on an isothermal plate as reported previously (Gray et al., 2005; Li et al., 2014; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), AIZ inhibition had no effect on the expected thermotaxis behavior of either fed or starved animals (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by thermotaxis bias data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: While starvation inhibits activity in both AIA and AIZ, complete suppression of these responses in AIA but not AIZ disrupts negative thermotaxis regardless of feeding state.
source: We conclude that while starvation inhibits activity in both AIA and AIZ, complete suppression of these responses in AIA but not AIZ disrupts negative thermotaxis regardless of feeding state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging and manipulation experiments on AIA and AIZ.

claim: Activation of AIA was sufficient to restore the ability of starved animals to perform negative thermotaxis.
source: Activation of AIA was sufficient to restore the ability of starved animals to perform negative thermotaxis (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: AWC inhibits AIA via glutamatergic signaling.
source: AWC inhibits AIA via glutamatergic signaling (Chalasani et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chalasani et al., 2010.

claim: Knocking out the glutamate transporter eat-4 cell-specifically in AWC resulted in robust negative thermotaxis behavior by starved animals.
source: Indeed, we found that knocking out the glutamate transporter eat-4 cell-specifically in AWC (López-Cruz et al., 2019) resulted in robust negative thermotaxis behavior by starved animals (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data with AWC-specific eat-4 knockout shown in Figure 3I and citation to López-Cruz et al., 2019.

claim: Upon prolonged starvation, increased AWC temperature responses inhibit AIA via glutamatergic signaling to disrupt negative thermotaxis via warming-uncorrelated regulation of reversals and turns.
source: These experiments suggest that upon prolonged starvation, increased AWC temperature responses inhibit AIA via glutamatergic signaling to disrupt negative thermotaxis via warming-uncorrelated regulation of reversals and turns.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AWC and AIA manipulation and imaging experiments.

claim: Suppression or activation of AIA in fed or starved animals is sufficient to permit or inhibit negative thermotaxis, respectively.
source: Moreover, these observations indicate that suppression or activation of AIA in fed or starved animals is sufficient to permit or inhibit negative thermotaxis, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AIA manipulation experiments.

claim: ins-1 has been shown to be expressed in multiple neuron types, including AIA as well as in the intestine.
source: ins-1 has previously been shown to be expressed in multiple neuron types, including AIA as well as in the intestine, as assessed via GFP reporter expression under ins-1 regulatory sequences (Kodama et al., 2006; Pierce et al., 2001; Tomioka et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kodama et al., 2006; Pierce et al., 2001; Tomioka et al., 2006.

claim: Knocking out ins-1 in all or a majority of ins-1-expressing cells restored negative thermotaxis in starved animals.
source: Knocking out ins-1 in all or a majority of ins-1-expressing cells by driving Cre::SL2::GFP under endogenous ins-1 regulatory sequences restored negative thermotaxis in starved animals, similar to the behavior of ins-1 null mutants (Figure 4A and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-specific knockout data shown in Figure 4A and D.

claim: Animals in which ins-1 was deleted only in AIA or AIZ/AIB failed to perform negative thermotaxis upon starvation.
source: However, animals in which ins-1 was deleted only in AIA or AIZ/AIB via Cre::SL2::GFP expression under the gcy-28d or odr-2b(3a) promoters, respectively failed to perform negative thermotaxis upon starvation.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-specific knockout data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Knocking out ins-1 specifically in the intestine was sufficient to rescue the negative thermotaxis behavioral defect in starved animals.
source: In contrast, knocking out ins-1 specifically in the intestine via Cre::SL2::GFP driven under the ifb-2 promoter was again sufficient to rescue the negative thermotaxis behavioral defect in starved animals (Figure 4A; Kodama et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by intestine-specific knockout data shown in Figure 4A and citation to Kodama et al., 2006.

claim: ins-1 production from the intestine is necessary for starvation-mediated plasticity in negative thermotaxis.
source: These results indicate that ins-1 production from the intestine is necessary for starvation-mediated plasticity in negative thermotaxis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell-specific knockout experiments.

claim: Levels of ins-1p::GFP::PEST expression in the gut were not altered upon food deprivation for 3 hr.
source: However, levels of ins-1p::GFP::PEST expression in the gut were not altered upon food deprivation for 3 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Animals mutant for the age-1 and akt-1 kinases exhibited phenotypes similar to those of wild-type animals, such that they failed to perform negative thermotaxis upon starvation.
source: We found that animals mutant for the age-1 and akt-1 kinases in this pathway exhibited phenotypes similar to those of wild-type animals, such that they failed to perform negative thermotaxis upon starvation (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Loss of function of the daf-18 PTEN phosphatase and daf-16 FOXO restored the ability of starved animals to perform negative thermotaxis.
source: In contrast, loss of function of the daf-18 PTEN phosphatase and daf-16 FOXO restored the ability of starved animals to perform negative thermotaxis, similar to the phenotype of ins-1 mutants (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Starvation inhibits the ILP signaling pathway and phosphorylation of DAF-16 to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
source: These observations imply that starvation inhibits the ILP signaling pathway and phosphorylation of DAF-16 to disrupt negative thermotaxis (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic analysis of the insulin signaling pathway components.

claim: Loss of daf-2 function did not further affect starvation-mediated loss of negative thermotaxis.
source: Consistent with the notion that DAF-2-mediated signaling is inhibited upon starvation, loss of daf-2 function did not further affect starvation-mediated loss of negative thermotaxis (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Upon starvation, INS-1 directly or indirectly antagonizes DAF-2 and disrupts negative thermotaxis via DAF-16.
source: We infer that upon starvation, INS-1 directly or indirectly antagonizes DAF-2 and disrupts negative thermotaxis via DAF-16.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic analysis of the insulin signaling pathway.

claim: Addition of auxin during the 3 hr starvation period and the assay but not during the assay alone resulted in significant rescue of negative thermotaxis behavior upon DAF-16 depletion in AWC.
source: We found that addition of auxin during the 3 hr starvation period and the assay but not during the assay alone resulted in significant rescue of negative thermotaxis behavior (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by auxin-induced degradation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: INS-1 targets DAF-16 in AWC to modulate negative thermotaxis bias as a function of feeding state.
source: We infer that INS-1 targets DAF-16 in AWC to modulate negative thermotaxis bias as a function of feeding state, and that DAF-16 function is necessary during prolonged starvation for this modulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the AWC-specific DAF-16 depletion experiments.

claim: DAF-16 function is necessary during prolonged starvation for modulation of negative thermotaxis.
source: We infer that INS-1 targets DAF-16 in AWC to modulate negative thermotaxis bias as a function of feeding state, and that DAF-16 function is necessary during prolonged starvation for this modulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing of auxin addition in the DAF-16 depletion experiments.

claim: In contrast to the increased activity in AWC observed in starved wild-type animals, temperature responses in AWC were no longer modulated by feeding state in ins-1 mutants.
source: Indeed, we found that in contrast to the increased activity in AWC observed in starved wild-type animals, temperature responses in this neuron type were no longer modulated by feeding state in ins-1 mutants (Figure 4F and H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data in ins-1 mutants shown in Figure 4F and H, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: AWC neurons in both fed and starved ins-1 mutants exhibited infrequent responses similar to the response profiles of fed wild-type animals.
source: Specifically, AWC neurons in both fed and starved ins-1 mutants exhibited infrequent responses similar to the response profiles of fed wild-type animals (Figure 4F and H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4F and H, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The proportion of responding animals, the total response duration per neuron, as well as the average duration of individual events in AIA in fed and starved ins-1 mutants resembled the activity profiles of AIA neurons in fed wild-type animals.
source: Similarly, the proportion of responding animals, the total response duration per neuron, as well as the average duration of individual events in AIA in fed and starved ins-1 mutants resembled the activity profiles of AIA neurons in fed wild-type animals (Figure 4G–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4G–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2F.

claim: INS-1 signaling in starved animals alters AWC and AIA temperature responses to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
source: We conclude that INS-1 signaling in starved animals alters AWC and AIA temperature responses to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging experiments in ins-1 mutants.

claim: Prolonged starvation disrupts negative thermotaxis by altering the activity of the modulatory AWC-AIA, but not that of the core thermosensory AFD-AIY, circuit.
source: We show here that prolonged starvation disrupts negative thermotaxis by altering the activity of the modulatory AWC-AIA, but not that of the core thermosensory AFD-AIY, circuit.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the Discussion, supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: In fed animals, warming fails to evoke responses in AWC.
source: In fed animals, warming fails to evoke responses in AWC.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2C.

claim: In fed animals, AIA exhibits tonic activity and inhibits reversals and turns, thereby enabling AFD-driven regulation of klinokinesis and turning bias as a function of temperature changes and the animal's Tc.
source: Under these conditions, AIA exhibits tonic activity and inhibits reversals and turns, thereby enabling AFD-driven regulation of klinokinesis and turning bias as a function of temperature changes and the animal's Tc (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by calcium imaging and behavioral data, and illustrated in Figure 4I.

claim: During prolonged food deprivation, INS-1 signaling from the gut acts via DAF-16 in AWC neurons to alter their response properties.
source: However, during prolonged food deprivation, INS-1 signaling from the gut acts via DAF-16 in AWC neurons to alter their response properties.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by the cell-specific knockout and auxin-induced degradation experiments.

claim: The altered state of AWC in starved animals results in enhanced temperature responses in AWC, and consequent disruption of AFD-driven thermotactic navigation via suppression of AIA activity.
source: The altered state of AWC in starved animals results in enhanced temperature responses in AWC, and consequent disruption of AFD-driven thermotactic navigation via suppression of AIA activity (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by the calcium imaging and manipulation experiments, and illustrated in Figure 4I.

claim: The activity state of AWC-AIA is permissive for AFD-dependent negative thermotaxis in fed animals.
source: Our results indicate that the activity state of AWC-AIA is permissive for AFD-dependent negative thermotaxis in fed animals, and that food deprivation modulates AWC-AIA via gut-to-brain signaling to disrupt this behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion, supported by the experimental data.

claim: Food deprivation modulates AWC-AIA via gut-to-brain signaling to disrupt negative thermotaxis behavior.
source: Our results indicate that the activity state of AWC-AIA is permissive for AFD-dependent negative thermotaxis in fed animals, and that food deprivation modulates AWC-AIA via gut-to-brain signaling to disrupt this behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion, supported by the intestine-specific ins-1 knockout experiments.

claim: Starvation has been shown to enhance odorant responses in AWC.
source: Starvation has previously been shown to enhance odorant responses in AWC (Neal et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Neal et al., 2015.

claim: Starvation-dependent changes in sensory responses in AWC allow C. elegans to prioritize responses to bacterial food-related odorants over optimal thermoregulation.
source: We speculate that starvation-dependent changes in sensory responses in AWC allow C. elegans to prioritize responses to bacterial food-related odorants over optimal thermoregulation.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion.

claim: INS-1 signaling from the gut is necessary to modulate AWC responses upon prolonged starvation possibly via altered processing and/or release.
source: We find that INS-1 signaling from the gut is necessary to modulate AWC responses upon prolonged starvation possibly via altered processing and/or release.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by the intestine-specific knockout experiments and the observation that ins-1 expression levels don't change.

claim: Expression of ins-1 specifically in AIA has been shown to be sufficient for modulation of chemosensory responses in AWC as well as in the ASER sensory neurons upon pairing starvation with AWC- or ASE-sensed chemical cues.
source: In contrast, ins-1 expression in AIA has been shown to be sufficient for modulation of chemosensory responses in AWC as well as in the ASER sensory neurons upon pairing starvation with AWC- or ASE-sensed chemical cues (Chalasani et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2010; Tomioka et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chalasani et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2010; Tomioka et al., 2006.

claim: Expression of ins-1 from multiple neuron types rescues the ins-1 thermotaxis behavioral phenotype in starved animals.
source: Similarly, expression of ins-1 from multiple neuron types rescues the ins-1 thermotaxis behavioral phenotype in starved animals (Kodama et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kodama et al., 2006.

claim: While ins-1 overexpression from multiple neuronal sources including AIA is sufficient, expression and/or production from specific cells and tissues, potentially at different levels, and in response to changing internal states over time, may be necessary for neuromodulation in AWC.
source: These observations suggest that while ins-1 overexpression from multiple neuronal sources including AIA is sufficient, expression and/or production from specific cells and tissues, potentially at different levels, and in response to changing internal states over time, may be necessary for neuromodulation in AWC.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion based on the comparison of sufficiency and necessity experiments.

claim: The expression of multiple ILP genes as well as neuropeptides is regulated by diverse environmental and internal conditions in different cell types in C. elegans.
source: The expression of multiple ILP genes as well as neuropeptides is regulated by diverse environmental and internal conditions in different cell types in C. elegans (Cornils et al., 2011; Fernandes de Abreu et al., 2014; Kim and Li, 2004; Pierce et al., 2001; Ritter et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cornils et al., 2011; Fernandes de Abreu et al., 2014; Kim and Li, 2004; Pierce et al., 2001; Ritter et al., 2013.

claim: Regulated transcription and/or release of ILPs and other peptides from defined cell and tissue types is likely critical for modulation of specific neuron types as a function of temporally varying internal states.
source: It is likely that regulated transcription and/or release of ILPs and other peptides from defined cell and tissue types is critical for modulation of specific neuron types as a function of temporally varying internal states.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion.

claim: AWC responses to a steeply rising temperature stimulus are time-locked.
source: However, AWC responses to a steeply rising temperature stimulus are time-locked (Kuhara et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kuhara et al., 2008.

claim: ASER salt-sensing neurons exhibit stochastic activity in response to a shallow linear salt gradient.
source: Similarly, while the ASER salt-sensing neurons exhibit stochastic activity in response to a shallow linear salt gradient, they exhibit time-locked responses when subjected to large step changes in salt concentrations (Luo et al., 2014b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2014b.

claim: ASER neurons exhibit time-locked responses when subjected to large step changes in salt concentrations.
source: Similarly, while the ASER salt-sensing neurons exhibit stochastic activity in response to a shallow linear salt gradient, they exhibit time-locked responses when subjected to large step changes in salt concentrations (Luo et al., 2014b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2014b.

claim: A shallow thermal ramp may not be sufficient to elicit sustained temperature responses in AWC, resulting in the observed stochastic activity pattern.
source: We suggest that a shallow thermal ramp may not be sufficient to elicit sustained temperature responses in AWC, resulting in the observed stochastic activity pattern.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion.

claim: Upon prolonged starvation, DAF-16-regulated expression changes in as yet unidentified thermosensory signaling molecules in AWC may lead to the observed increased frequency and duration of temperature response.
source: Upon prolonged starvation, DAF-16-regulated expression changes in as yet unidentified thermosensory signaling molecules in AWC may lead to the observed increased frequency and duration of temperature response.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion.

claim: CMK-1 calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase I and EGL-4 cGMP-dependent protein kinase have been implicated in regulating AWC olfactory responses as a function of starvation in distinct contexts.
source: Molecules such as the CMK-1 calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase I and the EGL-4 cGMP-dependent protein kinase have previously been implicated in regulating AWC olfactory responses as a function of starvation in distinct contexts (Cho et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2010; Neal et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cho et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2010; Neal et al., 2015.

claim: Distinct pathways may translate internal state information into changes in AWC responses under different conditions.
source: Molecules such as the CMK-1 calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase I and the EGL-4 cGMP-dependent protein kinase have previously been implicated in regulating AWC olfactory responses as a function of starvation in distinct contexts (Cho et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2010; Neal et al., 2015), suggesting that distinct pathways may translate internal state information into changes in AWC responses under different conditions.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion based on the cited studies.

claim: The circuit underlying thermotaxis behaviors in C. elegans is remarkably degenerate, and alternate neuronal pathways can compensate for the absence of the core AFD and AIY components in distinct contexts for different aspects of thermotaxis behaviors.
source: The circuit underlying thermotaxis behaviors in C. elegans is remarkably degenerate, and alternate neuronal pathways can compensate for the absence of the core AFD and AIY components in distinct contexts for different aspects of thermotaxis behaviors (Beverly et al., 2011; Matsuyama and Mori, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Beverly et al., 2011; Matsuyama and Mori, 2020.

claim: AIZ may be a component of a degenerate circuit that modulates negative thermotaxis under specific environmental or genetic conditions.
source: AIZ may be a component of a degenerate circuit that modulates negative thermotaxis under specific environmental or genetic conditions.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion.

claim: The presence of degenerate circuits driving specific behaviors in a context-dependent manner is a conserved feature of nervous systems, and contributes to both robustness and flexibility in behavioral outputs.
source: Although this hypothesis remains to be verified, the presence of degenerate circuits driving specific behaviors in a context-dependent manner is a conserved feature of nervous systems, and contributes to both robustness and flexibility in behavioral outputs (Cropper et al., 2016; Edelman and Gally, 2001; Prinz et al., 2004; Saideman et al., 2007; Trojanowski et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cropper et al., 2016; Edelman and Gally, 2001; Prinz et al., 2004; Saideman et al., 2007; Trojanowski et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019.

claim: Acute inhibition of AWC and activation of AIA is sufficient to restore negative thermotaxis in starved animals, indicating that the functions of the core thermotaxis circuit are maintained, but are masked by the activity state of the AWC-AIA circuit.
source: Acute inhibition of AWC and activation of AIA is sufficient to restore negative thermotaxis in starved animals, indicating that the functions of the core thermotaxis circuit are maintained, but are masked by the activity state of the AWC-AIA circuit.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by the manipulation experiments in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The activity state of the ASG sensory neurons is permissive for avoidance of starvation-associated low salt concentrations by the ASER salt-sensing neurons in C. elegans.
source: Recently, it has been shown that the activity state of the ASG sensory neurons is similarly permissive for avoidance of starvation-associated low salt concentrations by the ASER salt-sensing neurons in C. elegans (Jang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jang et al., 2019.

claim: Incorporating distinct modulatory pathways as a function of different experiences and conditions allows for a greater degree of behavioral flexibility and more efficient behavioral reprioritization, as compared to direct modulation of the core circuit itself, particularly in small circuits.
source: We suggest that incorporating distinct modulatory pathways as a function of different experiences and conditions allows for a greater degree of behavioral flexibility and more efficient behavioral reprioritization, as compared to direct modulation of the core circuit itself, particularly in small circuits.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion.

claim: Food deprivation for different periods of time has been shown to result in distinct behavioral changes that may be physiologically relevant in terms of driving specific food-seeking behaviors.
source: Food deprivation for different periods of time has been shown to result in distinct behavioral changes that may be physiologically relevant in terms of driving specific food-seeking behaviors (Churgin et al., 2017; Farhadian et al., 2012; Ghosh et al., 2016; Gray et al., 2005; Inagaki et al., 2014; Lee and Park, 2004; López-Cruz et al., 2019; Neal et al., 2015; Root et al., 2011; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Churgin et al., 2017; Farhadian et al., 2012; Ghosh et al., 2016; Gray et al., 2005; Inagaki et al., 2014; Lee and Park, 2004; López-Cruz et al., 2019; Neal et al., 2015; Root et al., 2011; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003.

claim: Behavioral changes due to food deprivation may be driven via temporally regulated recruitment of different neuronal pathways to functionally reconfigure the core sensorimotor circuit and reprioritize behaviors.
source: These changes may be driven via temporally regulated recruitment of different neuronal pathways to functionally reconfigure the core sensorimotor circuit and reprioritize behaviors (Churgin et al., 2017; Ghosh et al., 2016; Gray et al., 2005; Inagaki et al., 2012; Saeki et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Churgin et al., 2017; Ghosh et al., 2016; Gray et al., 2005; Inagaki et al., 2012; Saeki et al., 2001.

claim: Modulatory pathways primarily target sensory neurons and first layer interneurons in C. elegans presumably due to the relatively shallow network architecture of the nematode nervous system.
source: Although modulatory pathways may target different nodes in the underlying circuits, sensory neurons and first layer interneurons are the primary targets in C. elegans presumably due to the relatively shallow network architecture of the nematode nervous system.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference based on the architecture of the C. elegans nervous system.

claim: Functional reconfiguration of circuits via neuromodulation expands the repertoire of circuit outputs.
source: Functional reconfiguration of circuits via neuromodulation expands the repertoire of circuit outputs (Bargmann, 2012; Griffith, 2013; Kim et al., 2017; Marder, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bargmann, 2012; Griffith, 2013; Kim et al., 2017; Marder, 2012.

claim: Identification of the pathway by which internal state regulates thermotaxis behavioral plasticity in C. elegans adds to our understanding of the mechanistic richness of neuromodulator functions.
source: Identification of the pathway by which internal state regulates thermotaxis behavioral plasticity in C. elegans adds to our understanding of the mechanistic richness of neuromodulator functions, and suggests that related principles may operate across diverse sensory circuits.
evidence: This is a concluding statement in the Discussion.

claim: Related principles of neuromodulation may operate across diverse sensory circuits.
source: Identification of the pathway by which internal state regulates thermotaxis behavioral plasticity in C. elegans adds to our understanding of the mechanistic richness of neuromodulator functions, and suggests that related principles may operate across diverse sensory circuits.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion.
